tagline: A true thing, torn and re-set in a strict grid, dries into words a stranger can trust by night.

epigraph.text: The report of my death was an exaggeration.
epigraph.cite: Mark Twain, to the New York Journal, 1897

art.note: The council chose to keep the Rebel's fibrous tears and editing scars inside a strict 1:1.618 grid, replacing hand-pasted chaos with a procedural 60 BPM iron-gall settle and a single #c8102e wet edge.

writers.note: The council's voice is a 60 BPM newsroom clock: exact, ink-stained, and honest enough to earn a stranger's trust.

nuggets.hook: A fact is only news after it survives six questions.
nuggets.body: Before the ink settles, every claim asks who, what, when, where, why, and how. The answers become the story's spine.

nuggets.hook: Forty words decide whether a stranger keeps reading.
nuggets.body: The first sentence must carry the biggest fact, the clearest name, and the least waste. If it wobbles, the rest of the page feels suspicious.

nuggets.hook: The most important fact gets the shortest room.
nuggets.body: The upside-down pyramid puts the core event at the top and the context below. A reader can stop at any line and still trust the shape.

nuggets.hook: Old ink, new power: newspapers can change a nation.
nuggets.body: From hand-presses to muckrakers, the press became a machine for checking power. Its speed made it dangerous, and its errors made it human.
